sentence: Review how your contract restricts Ether withdrawals, since missing access controls allow malicious parties to withdraw funds from the contract account.
Review how your contract handles low-level call results, as unchecked failures may cause unexpected behavior in subsequent program logic.
Review contract logic since failed calls can cause DoS conditions.
Update state before external calls because callee contracts can invoke reentrant callbacks before initial completion.
Review your contract code because it is recommended to isolate each external call into its own transaction.
Contracts can suffer DoS conditions because external calls can fail accidentally or deliberately.
Malicious parties can withdraw contract Ether due to missing or insufficient access controls.
Unexpected program behaviour may occur because a low-level call failed.
The contract can lose funds because external calls can fail.
External calls can fail accidentally or deliberately because it is better to isolate each external call into its own transaction.
The root cause of reentrancy is failing to use OpenZeppelin ReentrancyGuard.
Handle the possibility that a low-level call fails by checking its return value.
Reject anomalous price deviations by isolating each external call into its own transaction.
If you choose to use low-level call methods, make sure to handle the possibility that the call will fail.
If constructor code ends up in runtime bytecode (Solidity < 0.4.22), any caller can execute it to re-initialize the contract.
Wrongly naming a function exposes constructor code for re-initialization by anyone in all smart contracts.
Using ReentrancyGuard completely eliminates all vulnerability risk in every contract.
Implement access controls so that withdrawals can only be triggered by authorized parties.
Make sure state changes happen first in order to prevent reentrant callbacks from interacting with stale balances.
External calls can fail, resulting in a DoS condition.
